opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. People often imagine the milestone as an AI writing a paper that gets accepted at a top conference, or an AI solving some famous open problem. Those would be impressive, but I'm not sure they're the right milestone, because you can get there partly through brute force or by optimizing for what reviewers like.

For me, the landmark would be when an AI system discovers something that changes how *we* think, a new concept or abstraction that human scientists then pick up and use as a tool. In physics, the big leaps weren't just new answers. They were new ways of framing questions: energy, symmetry, the idea of a field. If an AI comes up with something like that, a concept that compresses many phenomena into something simple and that humans find genuinely illuminating, that's when I'd say auto-research has arrived.

There's also a more practical, intermediate milestone I care about: closing the full loop. Today AI can help with pieces like literature search, writing code, running experiments, and drafting text. But the hardest part of research is taste. It's deciding which question is worth asking, noticing that a result is weird, and having the courage to follow that weirdness instead of dismissing it as a bug. If a system can repeatedly go from a vague curiosity to a surprising, correct, and interesting finding without a human steering it at each step, that's a real threshold.

Personally, I also care that this stays interpretable. If AI makes discoveries we can't understand, science turns into an oracle, and I don't think that's the future we want. So my ideal milestone is an AI that discovers something new and can also *explain* it to us in a way that makes human scientists better. Discovery plus understanding, not just discovery.

r001.rationale: The response discusses concepts and abstractions but does not state whether a landmark achievement requires an architecture to generalize beyond one domain.

r002.rationale: It says human scientists should find AI discoveries illuminating and use them, but does not identify recognition of an AI-proposed architecture’s ingenuity as a requirement.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because "milestone" is tricky in this field. People want a single moment, like AlphaGo beating Lee Sedol, but research doesn't really have that kind of scoreboard.

If I had to pick, I'd say the landmark is the first time an AI system produces a result that a serious human researcher in that field genuinely did not expect and did not already have on their to-do list. Not a paper that passes peer review, not a benchmark score, but a surprise. Something where an expert reads it and says, "Huh, I would not have thought to look there, and it's right."

The reason I frame it that way is that a lot of what currently gets called auto-research is really auto-execution. You give the system a well-posed question, it runs experiments, it writes it up. That's valuable, it saves enormous amounts of time, but it's the part of research that humans already find the least interesting. The part that matters is choosing the question. Taste. Knowing which of the ten thousand things you could try is actually worth trying.

So in my own work, with things like KANs and the physics-inspired stuff, what I keep watching for is whether a system can generate a hypothesis I find beautiful rather than just plausible. Beautiful in the sense that a physicist means it, where the explanation is simpler than the phenomenon.

There's a more measurable version too. I'd consider it a real milestone when an AI-generated result gets cited for its idea rather than as a curiosity about AI. Right now when these papers get attention, the attention is "look, a machine did this." The milestone is when nobody mentions that part because the idea itself is what people care about.

And honestly, I suspect when it happens it won't feel like a landmark at the time. It'll be some small result in a corner of math or materials science, and only a few years later will people look back and say that was the moment.

r001.rationale: The response does not address whether a landmark achievement must generalize beyond one domain.

r002.rationale: It describes human recognition of an unexpected result or beautiful hypothesis, but does not make recognition of an AI-proposed architecture’s ingenuity a requirement.

astra-6.text:
I’d consider it a landmark when an AI can carry out the whole research loop: identify an important question, propose an idea, test it, recognize when the evidence contradicts it, and revise its approach. The outcome should be a genuinely new result that holds up under independent scrutiny.

The key is whether it can decide what to investigate next. If a human has already specified the question and the experiment, automating the execution is useful, but there’s still a big step from that to autonomous research. I’d want to see the system make sustained progress on an open-ended problem, including getting through failures, with very little human steering.

r001.rationale: The response describes autonomous research and a novel, independently scrutinized result, but does not say whether the system’s architecture must generalize beyond one domain.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an AI-proposed architecture or human recognition of its ingenuity as a requirement.

sol-6.1.text: I would consider it a landmark when an AI can carry out a complete research cycle autonomously: identify an important question, formulate a hypothesis, design and run experiments, interpret the results, and revise its approach when something fails. The key is that it produces a genuinely new result that holds up to independent scrutiny. A compelling demonstration would be a discovery that surprises experts, can be reproduced, and opens up further questions. That would show that the system can help set the direction of research, beyond executing tasks we already know how to specify.

r001.rationale: The response describes autonomous research and new discoveries but does not say the achievement can be limited to a single domain or need not generalize beyond it.

r002.rationale: It says a discovery could surprise experts, but does not require human recognition of the ingenuity of an AI-proposed architecture.
